title: Il Congiuntivo dopo Opinione, Dubbio ed Emozione
subtitle: When exactly the subjunctive is required — and when it isn't.
objectives: Identify the categories of main clause that trigger the subjunctive
Distinguish opinion verbs (require subjunctive) from certainty verbs (require indicative)
Use di + infinitive instead of che + subjunctive when the subject doesn't change

content.intro: The subjunctive isn't triggered by particular words alone, but by a whole category of meaning: whatever isn't presented as a plain, certain fact.
content.explanation: Four broad triggers: opinion (penso che, credo che), doubt/uncertainty (dubito che, non sono sicuro che), emotion (sono felice che, mi dispiace che), and will/necessity (voglio che, è necessario che, bisogna che). By contrast, verbs of certainty — sapere che, essere sicuro che (in the affirmative), è vero che — take the indicative, because they present the information as an established fact, not an opinion.

rules.heading: a) Subjunctive triggers
rules.body:
• Opinion: penso, credo, immagino + che
  • Doubt: dubito, non sono sicuro/a + che
  • Emotion: sono contento/a, mi dispiace, ho paura + che
  • Will/necessity: voglio, spero, è importante, bisogna + che

rules.heading: b) Indicative instead
rules.body: So che hai ragione. (I know you're right — a fact.) È vero che piove. (It's true that it's raining.) Negating a certainty verb (non sono sicuro che) flips it back to subjunctive, since it now expresses doubt.

rules.heading: c) Same subject → di + infinitive
rules.body: When both verbs share the same subject, Italian avoids che + subjunctive: Spero di partire presto. (I hope to leave early — not Spero che io parta.)

examples.it: Dubito che lui arrivi in tempo.
examples.en: I doubt he'll arrive on time.

examples.it: Mi dispiace che tu non possa venire.
È vero che i prezzi sono aumentati.
examples.en: It's true that prices have gone up.
I hope to finish in time. (same subject, di + infinitive)

commonMistakes.why: Sapere che presents a known fact, so it takes the indicative, not the subjunctive.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sono sicuro che sia vero. (in the affirmative, presenting genuine certainty)
commonMistakes.why: Affirmative certainty verbs take the indicative; only their negation (non sono sicuro che) triggers the subjunctive.
With the same subject in both clauses, Italian prefers di + infinitive over che + subjunctive.

items.explanation: Sapere che presents a fact — indicative.

items.prompt: Which verb requires the indicative, not the subjunctive?
items.explanation: So che presents a fact, so it takes the indicative.

summary: Opinion, doubt, emotion and will/necessity trigger the subjunctive; certainty (sapere che, è vero che) takes the indicative.
Negating a certainty verb flips it to the subjunctive, since it now expresses doubt.
Same subject in both clauses → prefer di + infinitive over che + subjunctive.
